title: CLARA: Clarification of Language Ambiguity through Result Analysis for Natural-Language Cancer Genomics Queries
comment: Preprint of an article submitted for consideration in the Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing (PSB 2027). Copyright 2026 World Scientific Publishing Company. https://psb.stanford.edu/
summary: A natural language interface can be used to make cancer genomics databases easier to use, but even if a question is perfectly fluent, its scientific meaning can be ambiguous. We propose CLARA, a framework that represents a question as a typed scientific query specification, considers a few possible interpretations, executes them, and asks for clarification when the estimates diverge. CLARA was assessed on mutation-prevalence contrasts among eight TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts and a 30-gene panel. This benchmark consisted of 330 unique executable contrasts varying in mutation scope, assay denominator, and sample context; 115 contrasts were result-sensitive and 215 were result-stable, per the preregistered definition of relative divergence greater than 0.10 or absolute divergence greater than 5 percentage points. An independently implemented pandas execution engine perfectly replicated all 660 results from the SQLite engine. In a separate 120-question LLM-generated, manually vetted language stress test, CLARA recognized all 60 result-sensitive contrasts and needlessly clarified 13 of 60 stable contrasts (accuracy 89.2%, sensitivity/recall 100%, specificity 78.3%). Standalone machine learning had superior overall accuracy (97.5%) but missed one critical contrast. This demonstrates that downstream execution can distinguish consequential from inconsequential ambiguity and reveal an explicit trade-off between safety and burden.

AI.tldr: CLARA is a framework for natural language interfaces to cancer genomics databases that represents questions as typed scientific query specifications, executes multiple possible interpretations, and asks for clarification when results diverge. It was validated on a benchmark of 330 executable mutation-prevalence contrasts and a 120-question language stress test, achieving 89.2% accuracy with 100% sensitivity while trading off safety against user burden.
AI.motivation: Natural language interfaces make cancer genomics databases more accessible, but perfectly fluent questions can still have ambiguous scientific meaning. The ambiguity can be consequential or inconsequential, and there is a need to distinguish between the two.
AI.method: CLARA represents a question as a typed scientific query specification, considers a few possible interpretations, executes them (via SQLite engine), and asks for clarification when the estimates diverge. The framework was benchmarked on mutation-prevalence contrasts among eight TCGA PanCancer Atlas cohorts and a 30-gene panel, with a preregistered definition of relative divergence >0.10 or absolute divergence >5 percentage points to classify results as sensitive vs. stable.
AI.result: In the benchmark, 115 contrasts were result-sensitive and 215 were result-stable. An independent pandas engine perfectly replicated all 660 SQLite results. In a 120-question LLM-generated, manually vetted stress test, CLARA recognized all 60 result-sensitive contrasts and unnecessarily clarified 13 of 60 stable contrasts (accuracy 89.2%, sensitivity 100%, specificity 78.3%). Standalone machine learning achieved higher overall accuracy (97.5%) but missed one critical contrast.
AI.conclusion: Downstream execution can distinguish consequential from inconsequential ambiguity in natural language queries, revealing an explicit trade-off between safety (never missing critical contrasts) and burden (unnecessary clarifications). CLARA prioritizes safety, sacrificing some specificity compared to standalone machine learning approaches.

title: Frozen but Not Always Accessible: A Representation Analysis of Genomic Language Models
summary: Genomic foundation models are increasingly reused as frozen feature extractors for downstream sequence prediction, offering a compute-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning. However, it remains unclear when biological information encoded by these models is accessible without task-specific adaptation. We present a representation-accessibility analysis of frozen genomic language models across regulatory, epigenetic, promoter, splice-site, and variant-effect prediction tasks. We evaluate DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, HyenaDNA, GENERATOR-v2, and Omni-DNA under unified frozen-probing protocols, while separating diagnostic readout analyses from validation-selected checks. Our results reveal a consistent task-dependent pattern: frozen probes recover 95-100 % of fine-tuned performance on promoter tasks, but average splice-site recovery drops to 60-88 %. Frozen embeddings are also competitive on broad Genomic Benchmark tasks such as coding-region and species-discrimination classification, but show larger gaps on some regulatory and OCR tasks. Layer-wise probing, in-silico mutagenesis, variant-effect prediction, and embedding geometry show that local biological signal is partially present in frozen representations, but is not always accessible through final pooled embeddings.

AI.tldr: The paper systematically evaluates whether frozen genomic language model embeddings can access biological information without task-specific fine-tuning. Across diverse prediction tasks (regulatory, epigenetic, promoter, splice-site, variant-effect), frozen probes recover 95-100% of fine-tuned performance on promoter tasks but only 60-88% on splice-site tasks, revealing a consistent task-dependent pattern in representation accessibility.
AI.motivation: Genomic foundation models are increasingly reused as frozen feature extractors for downstream tasks to save compute, but it remains unclear when biologically relevant information encoded in these models is actually accessible without task-specific adaptation. Understanding this representation accessibility is crucial for deciding when frozen probing is sufficient versus when fine-tuning is necessary.
AI.method: The authors conduct a representation-accessibility analysis of five frozen genomic language models (DNABERT-2, Nucleotide Transformer, HyenaDNA, GENERATOR-v2, Omni-DNA) under unified frozen-probing protocols across regulatory, epigenetic, promoter, splice-site, and variant-effect prediction tasks. They separate diagnostic readout analyses from validation-selected checks, and employ layer-wise probing, in-silico mutagenesis, variant-effect prediction, and embedding geometry analysis.
AI.result: Frozen probes recover 95-100% of fine-tuned performance on promoter tasks, while splice-site recovery drops to 60-88%. Frozen embeddings are competitive on broad Genomic Benchmark tasks (coding-region and species-discrimination classification) but show larger gaps on regulatory and OCR tasks. Layer-wise and geometric analyses show local biological signal is partially present in frozen representations but not always accessible through final pooled embeddings.
AI.conclusion: The accessibility of biological information in frozen genomic representations is task-dependent: some tasks (e.g., promoters) have highly accessible representations, while others (e.g., splice sites) require fine-tuning. Local biological signal may exist in frozen representations but can be lost or obscured in the final pooled embeddings, highlighting the need for careful consideration of when frozen probing is appropriate.

title: IL-10 rs1800896 polymorphism predicts biochemical remission in IBD patients undergoing biologic therapy
comment: 22 pages; 2 main tables and 1 main figure; supplementary tables and figure included. Pre-peer-reviewed author manuscript. The final article was published in Immunology, 2026, volume 177, issue 2, pages 432-438
summary: Background. Genetic factors, including single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), may modulate disease course and therapeutic efficacy in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Aim. We investigated the association between four SNPs in cytokine genes and clinical phenotype as well as the response to molecular-targeted drugs in patients with IBD. Materials and Methods. A total of 197 IBD patients (142 Crohn's disease [CD], 55 ulcerative colitis [UC]) undergoing targeted treatment were enrolled. The SNPs analyzed were TNF-alpha rs1800629 (-308 G>A), TGF-beta rs1800471 (codon 10 C>T), IL-6 rs1800795 (-174 G>C), and IL-10 rs1800896 (-1082 G>A). Biochemical response at 12 months (T12) was defined as CRP <5.0 mg/L and fecal calprotectin <250 microg/g at T12, in the absence of ongoing corticosteroid therapy. Results. The IL-6 rs1800795 C allele was significantly associated with a younger age at diagnosis (p=0.049), while the TNF-alpha rs1800629 A allele was more frequently observed in patients with CD than UC (p=0.036). Among 134 patients included in the per-protocol analysis, 41.0% achieved biochemical remission at T12. The IL-10 rs1800896 variant allele was associated with remission (OR 2.15, 95% CI 1.03-4.44; p=0.041), and the association remained significant in multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 4.15, 95% CI 1.49-11.56; p=0.007). Conclusions. Genotyping of cytokine-related SNPs may help identify patients with distinct disease phenotypes and support personalized treatment strategies in IBD.

AI.tldr: This study genotyped four cytokine-related SNPs in 197 IBD patients to examine associations with clinical phenotype and molecular-targeted therapy response. The IL-10 rs1800896 variant allele was significantly associated with biochemical remission at 12 months, and the IL-6 rs1800795 C allele correlated with younger age at diagnosis, suggesting potential utility of cytokine genotyping for personalized IBD treatment.
AI.motivation: Genetic factors such as SNPs may modulate disease course and therapeutic efficacy in IBD patients, but their role in predicting response to molecular-targeted drugs remains understudied. Identifying genetic markers could enable more personalized treatment strategies.
AI.method: A total of 197 IBD patients (142 CD, 55 UC) undergoing targeted treatment were enrolled. Four SNPs were analyzed: TNF-alpha rs1800629, TGF-beta rs1800471, IL-6 rs1800795, and IL-10 rs1800896. Biochemical response at 12 months (T12) was defined as CRP <5.0 mg/L and fecal calprotectin <250 microg/g without ongoing corticosteroids. Statistical analysis included univariate and multivariable regression.
AI.result: The IL-6 rs1800795 C allele was associated with younger age at diagnosis (p=0.049), and the TNF-alpha rs1800629 A allele was more frequent in CD than UC (p=0.036). Among 134 patients in per-protocol analysis, 41.0% achieved biochemical remission. The IL-10 rs1800896 variant allele was associated with remission (OR 2.15, p=0.041), remaining significant in multivariable analysis (adjusted OR 4.15, p=0.007).
AI.conclusion: Genotyping of cytokine-related SNPs may help identify IBD patients with distinct disease phenotypes and support personalized treatment strategies. The IL-10 variant allele appears to be a promising predictor of biochemical remission in response to molecular-targeted therapy.

title: The ethics of artificial intelligence in the life sciences: Universality, cultural diversity and an architecture of care
summary: The life sciences and health research have started to benefit from artificial intelligence, which raises ethical concerns that are real but, we argue, not special. Any science should be governed by values that rest on how the human brain is built and socialised rather than anything distinct to artificial intelligence. Importantly, the human brain has a different, much less costly computational architecture than these machines. This is achieved through the orchestration of a global neuronal workspace, and through reward best described not as a quantity to be maximised but as a continuous cycle of wanting, liking and satiety. As such, this creates the deep tension running through the ethics of the human person, between the universality of ethical judgement and the diversity of morals. The brain networks of the global workspace and emotion are universally shared, but the diversity of content is shaped by epigenetic appropriation of the particulars of the physical, social and cultural world, which makes every person unique. Still, if we were to build machines on these principles rather than the present unaffordable reward maximisers, the question of their governance would change from restraint to upbringing. We set out the institutions such a future would require, together with the questions that remain open.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that ethical concerns about AI in life sciences/health research are real but not unique to AI. It proposes that governance of AI should be based on principles derived from human brain architecture—specifically the global neuronal workspace and the reward cycle of wanting, liking, and satiety—rather than the current reward-maximizing paradigm, suggesting a shift from restricting machines to "upbringing" them.
AI.motivation: To reframe the ethical debate around AI in science, arguing that AI ethics should be grounded in human brain architecture and values rather than being treated as a special category, and to propose a more affordable and biologically-inspired alternative to current reward-maximizing AI systems.
AI.method: Conceptual argument based on neuroscience: draws on the global neuronal workspace theory, the reward cycle (wanting, liking, satiety), and the tension between universal ethical judgment and diverse morals shaped by epigenetic and socio-cultural factors.
AI.result: Articulates a principled framework where governance of future machines built on human-brain principles would shift from restraint to upbringing, and outlines the institutional requirements and open questions for such a future.
AI.conclusion: AI ethics should not be treated as special; governance should be informed by human neuroscience and values, moving toward an upbringing-based model for machines, while acknowledging remaining open questions.

title: Effective pruning of task-trained recurrent neural networks using noisy fluctuations and connection rescaling
summary: The pruning of network connections is key to brain function but, despite its importance, there exist few biologically-plausible pruning rules with demonstrated good performance. In this work we evaluate noise-prune, a recently introduced unsupervised local pruning rule for recurrent networks that uses noisy fluctuations to determine the importance of connections. Noise-prune has previously only been empirically tested on random networks without a specific computational function. We show that noise-prune preserves task-performance in task-trained recurrent neural networks, greatly outperforming a strategy that only uses the magnitude of connections and performing on par with or exceeding a non-local strategy that uses second-order information. Rather than deterministically removing connections that fall below a certain threshold importance, noise-prune samples connections to preserve based on their importance and strengthens retained connections to preserve average synaptic strength. We show that this sampling and rescaling is essential to good performance, but that the optimal empirical degree of rescaling is lower than that predicted by the original theoretical argument. Our work thus validates noise-prune as a biologically-plausible pruning rule for functional recurrent network architectures and characterizes its optimal parameter settings.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates noise-prune, a biologically-plausible unsupervised local pruning rule for recurrent neural networks, showing it preserves task performance in task-trained RNNs, outperforms magnitude-based pruning, and matches or exceeds second-order non-local methods. The authors demonstrate that its sampling and rescaling mechanism is essential, though optimal rescaling is lower than theoretically predicted.
AI.motivation: There are few biologically-plausible pruning rules with demonstrated good performance despite the importance of connection pruning in brain function. Noise-prune had only been tested on random networks without specific computational function, so its applicability to functionally trained networks was unknown.
AI.method: The authors evaluate noise-prune on task-trained recurrent neural networks, comparing it against magnitude-based pruning and a non-local second-order information strategy. They investigate the mechanism of sampling connections to preserve based on importance and rescaling retained connections, testing different degrees of rescaling against theoretical predictions.
AI.result: Noise-prune preserves task performance in trained RNNs, greatly outperforming magnitude-based pruning and performing on par with or exceeding non-local second-order methods. The sampling and rescaling mechanism is essential, but the optimal empirical rescaling is lower than theoretically predicted.
AI.conclusion: Noise-prune is validated as a biologically-plausible pruning rule for functional recurrent network architectures, with characterized optimal parameter settings.

title: From Local Learning to Global Prediction Through Layered Surprise Cascades
summary: Hierarchical predictive coding proposes a compelling hypothesis of brain computation, suggesting that the cortex builds layered predictions to minimize surprise. Yet most models rely on error-coding neurons or generative modeling of unclear biological plausibility. Here, we examine a biologically plausible framework in which the functional goals of predictive coding emerge from local contrastive learning and simple activity cancellation. Building on recent machine learning advances, we present a recurrent variant of the Forward-Forward (FF) algorithm with an inverted objective that increases activity for negative data. This setup yields predictive representations across layers, capturing hallmark features of cortical computation such as top-down modulation and surprise signaling. Our results suggest that key principles of predictive coding can emerge from simple, local learning rules, offering a new bridge between neuroscience and machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a biologically plausible framework where predictive coding emerges from local contrastive learning using a recurrent variant of the Forward-Forward algorithm with an inverted objective, capturing cortical features like top-down modulation and surprise signaling.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical predictive coding is a compelling hypothesis for brain computation, but most existing models rely on error-coding neurons or generative modeling with unclear biological plausibility.
AI.method: The authors present a recurrent variant of the Forward-Forward (FF) algorithm with an inverted objective that increases activity for negative data, enabling predictive representations to emerge across layers through local contrastive learning and activity cancellation.
AI.result: The framework produces predictive representations across layers and captures hallmark features of cortical computation such as top-down modulation and surprise signaling.
AI.conclusion: Key principles of predictive coding can emerge from simple, local learning rules, offering a new bridge between neuroscience and machine learning.

title: Transcutaneous Spinal Cord Stimulation Disrupts Conscious Ankle Proprioception and Produces a More Constrained Locomotor Pattern in Unimpaired Adults
summary: Transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) modulates spinal sensorimotor circuits primarily through activation of afferent networks. While prior work has emphasized locomotor performance and spinal excitability, how tSCS affects conscious proprioceptive perception and the extent to which such effects parallel changes in locomotor control remain unclear. We investigated the acute and training-related effects of tSCS on ankle proprioception and gait in unimpaired adults (n = 14), with an independent control group (n = 14) completing identical proprioceptive training without stimulation. Proprioception was quantified using a bilateral robotic assessment of dynamic ankle localization ability (Crisscross), gross motor output using maximum dorsiflexion strength, and gait during normal and tandem treadmill walking using spatiotemporal, trunk-sway, and mediolateral center-of-mass (CoM) excursion measures. Acute tSCS increased ankle proprioceptive error (p < 0.001) while dorsiflexion strength was unchanged (p = 0.30). Gait shifted toward a modestly more constrained locomotor pattern, characterized by reduced step width and ML CoM excursion (p < 0.05). With continued training under stimulation, proprioceptive error decreased and, unlike the control group, the tSCS group showed progressive improvement that persisted after stimulation ended. Sagittal-plane gait measures recovered toward or beyond baseline, whereas mediolateral measures remained constrained, revealing a direction-dependent reorganization of locomotor control. Together, these findings show that tSCS influences multiple aspects of the sensorimotor control loop, disrupting conscious proprioception while reshaping locomotor behavior, and that the nervous system can adapt to altered afferent input through training.

AI.tldr: This study examined how transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation (tSCS) affects ankle proprioception and gait in unimpaired adults. Acute tSCS increased proprioceptive error while leaving strength unchanged, but shifted gait toward a more constrained pattern (reduced step width and mediolateral center-of-mass excursion). With continued training under stimulation, proprioceptive accuracy improved progressively and persisted after stimulation ended, while mediolateral gait measures remained constrained, revealing direction-dependent reorganization of sensorimotor control.
AI.motivation: While prior tSCS research has focused on locomotor performance and spinal excitability, it remains unclear how tSCS affects conscious proprioceptive perception and whether these effects parallel changes in locomotor control.
AI.method: Fourteen unimpaired adults received tSCS while completing ankle proprioception training, compared to 14 control participants who did identical proprioceptive training without stimulation. Proprioception was measured via bilateral robotic dynamic ankle localization (Crisscross), gross motor output via maximum dorsiflexion strength, and gait via spatiotemporal, trunk-sway, and mediolateral center-of-mass measures during normal and tandem treadmill walking. Both acute and training-related effects were assessed.
AI.result: Acute tSCS significantly increased ankle proprioceptive error (p < 0.001) without changing dorsiflexion strength (p = 0.30), and produced a more constrained locomotor pattern with reduced step width and ML CoM excursion (p < 0.05). With training, the tSCS group showed progressive improvement in proprioceptive error that persisted after stimulation ended, unlike controls. Sagittal-plane gait recovered or exceeded baseline while mediolateral measures remained constrained.
AI.conclusion: tSCS affects multiple elements of the sensorimotor control loop by disrupting conscious proprioception while reshaping locomotor behavior, and the nervous system can adapt to altered afferent input through training, suggesting potential implications for rehabilitation paradigms using tSCS.

title: A Low-Power Wearable Respiratory Sensor for Non-Invasive Stress Monitoring
comment: Code available at this URL: https://github.com/mohamad-hoseini/FSResp
summary: Respiration provides a continuously available window into physiological state and behavior. However, monitoring it outside controlled settings remains challenging because a wearable system must capture small body deformations while remaining comfortable, low power, and robust to changes in posture and motion. We present a compact non-invasive respiratory sensing system based on a force-sensitive resistor (FSR) embedded in an abdominal belt and integrated with a custom Bluetooth Low Energy acquisition board. The system combines a simple piezoresistive readout with a mechanical holder designed to transfer abdominal expansion to the sensor without analog amplification. We evaluate the complete sensing pipeline across multiple breathing patterns and body positions. In stationary settings, the recorded signals exhibit consistent amplitude changes and recurring peak-to-peak timing across breathing maneuvers; under light movement, these variations remain visible despite motion-induced baseline shifts. We further design a five-phase stress-induction protocol and collect respiratory recordings from 12 participants. Using interpretable time-domain features and standard classifiers, we examine whether the acquired signals distinguish relaxation from stress-induction phases. In this preliminary experiment, the best-performing model achieves 88.0% test accuracy, indicating that the extracted respiratory features distinguish stress-induced phases from relaxation phases in this dataset. Overall, our results show that the proposed platform enables real-time respiratory monitoring across diverse daily-life scenarios and captures respiratory changes that distinguish stress-induction from relaxation phases, supporting its potential for affective-computing applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a compact, non-invasive respiratory sensing system using an FSR embedded in an abdominal belt with a custom BLE acquisition board. It evaluates the system across breathing patterns and body positions, and demonstrates 88.0% test accuracy in distinguishing stress-induction from relaxation phases using time-domain features and standard classifiers in a 12-participant experiment.
AI.motivation: Monitoring respiration outside controlled settings is challenging because a wearable system must capture small body deformations while remaining comfortable, low power, and robust to posture/motion changes. Existing solutions lack this combination of properties for real-world use.
AI.method: The system uses a force-sensitive resistor (FSR) embedded in an abdominal belt, integrated with a custom Bluetooth Low Energy acquisition board. A piezoresistive readout with a mechanical holder transfers abdominal expansion to the sensor without analog amplification. Evaluation includes multiple breathing patterns and body positions, plus a five-phase stress-induction protocol with 12 participants using interpretable time-domain features and standard classifiers.
AI.result: Stationary signals show consistent amplitude changes and recurring peak-to-peak timing; variations remain visible under light movement despite baseline shifts. The best-performing classifier achieves 88.0% test accuracy in distinguishing stress-induction from relaxation phases.
AI.conclusion: The platform enables real-time respiratory monitoring across diverse daily-life scenarios and captures respiratory changes distinguishing stress-induction from relaxation phases, supporting its potential for affective-computing applications.

title: Curriculum Multiple Shooting for Robust Training of Neural and Universal Differential Equations
summary: Neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs) and universal differential equations (UDEs) provide flexible and popular frameworks for learning interpretable dynamical systems from noisy time-series data. However, training these models remains challenging, and versatile methods that robustly handle sparse and noisy data as well as partially observed models are lacking. To address this, we introduce curriculum multiple shooting (CMS), a general-purpose training strategy for fitting ordinary differential equation (ODE) models to time-series data by integrating curriculum learning with multiple shooting. Across twelve benchmarks spanning simulated and real data, and covering NODEs, UDEs, and mechanistic ODEs, CMS accelerates and stabilises training convergence, outperforms state-of-the-art training strategies, and ranks among the best methods in generalisation. Finally, we discuss possible explanations for the strong performance of CMS in light of contemporary theories of what makes training on time-series challenging.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces curriculum multiple shooting (CMS), a training strategy that combines curriculum learning with multiple shooting to fit ODE models (including NODEs, UDEs, and mechanistic ODEs) to noisy, sparse, and partially observed time-series data. Across twelve benchmarks, CMS accelerates and stabilizes training convergence, outperforms state-of-the-art training methods, and ranks among the best in generalization.
AI.motivation: Training neural ODEs and universal differential equations on noisy time-series data remains challenging. Existing methods lack versatility in handling sparse, noisy, and partially observed data, motivating the need for a robust and general-purpose training strategy.
AI.method: CMS integrates curriculum learning with multiple shooting—a training approach that decomposes long time-series into shorter segments (shooting) and progressively increases problem difficulty (curriculum) to improve convergence and stability.
AI.result: Across twelve benchmarks covering simulated and real data with NODEs, UDEs, and mechanistic ODEs, CMS accelerates and stabilizes training convergence, outperforms state-of-the-art training strategies, and ranks among the best in generalization.
AI.conclusion: CMS is a general-purpose, robust training strategy for fitting ODE models to challenging time-series data. The paper also discusses potential theoretical explanations for its strong performance in light of contemporary learning theory for time-series training.

title: Complexity and Stability of Neural Activity Across Aging and Neurodegenerative Disease
summary: Objective: EEG signals fluctuate continuously even within a fixed cognitive state, but an important question is whether the brain still reuses similar activity patterns to represent information over time. Methods: To address this, we model EEG as distributions of windowed activity patterns and quantify their temporal stability using Wasserstein distance, while intrinsic dimensionality captures representational complexity. Results: Across multi-task, lifespan, and clinical EEG datasets, we find that neural representations show constrained, condition-specific stability rather than unconstrained drift. Higher intrinsic dimensionality is consistently associated with lower stability, suggesting that richer representational spaces are less reproducible over time. Both measures exhibit reproducible spatial organization, with posterior regions showing higher dimensionality and lower stability than frontal regions. Healthy aging is characterized by increased dimensionality and reduced stability, whereas mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease show a joint collapse of both. Conclusions: These findings provide a distribution-level framework for understanding neural stability across cognition, aging, and disease. Significance: This framework offers a principled approach to quantifying neural representational stability, with potential utility as a sensitive biomarker for tracking cognitive aging and neurodegeneration in clinical settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a distribution-level framework to quantify the temporal stability of EEG neural representations using Wasserstein distance and intrinsic dimensionality, finding that representations show condition-specific stability (not unconstrained drift), that higher dimensionality correlates with lower stability, and that these measures distinguish healthy aging (increased dimensionality, reduced stability) from MCI/Alzheimer's (joint collapse of both).
AI.motivation: EEG signals fluctuate continuously even within a fixed cognitive state, raising the question of whether the brain reuses similar activity patterns to represent information over time. A quantitative framework is needed to assess whether neural representations remain stable or drift.
AI.method: Model EEG as distributions of windowed activity patterns, quantify temporal stability using Wasserstein distance, and capture representational complexity via intrinsic dimensionality. Apply across multi-task, lifespan, and clinical EEG datasets.
AI.result: Neural representations show constrained, condition-specific stability rather than unconstrained drift. Higher intrinsic dimensionality is consistently associated with lower stability. Both measures show reproducible spatial organization (posterior higher dimensionality/lower stability than frontal). Healthy aging shows increased dimensionality and reduced stability; MCI and Alzheimer's show a joint collapse of both measures.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a distribution-level framework for understanding neural stability across cognition, aging, and disease, with potential utility as a sensitive biomarker for tracking cognitive aging and neurodegeneration in clinical settings.

title: Convergent Evolution in Algorithmic Space
summary: In evolutionary biology, unrelated organisms can independently evolve similar structures when exposed to similar functional demands. Here we ask whether an analogous form of convergent evolution occurs during neural network training: do networks with different random initializations develop similar internal weight structures when trained on the same task? This question is technically nontrivial because hidden neurons can be arbitrarily permuted without changing the represented function, making direct matrix comparisons misleading. We introduce a matching-based framework for comparing multilayer perceptrons in structural weight space. Hidden neurons are first coarsely aligned using permutation-invariant features and then refined by iterative Hungarian matching. After alignment, networks are compared with structural distance metrics designed to emphasize task-relevant weight patterns. Applying this approach to ensembles of small MLPs trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST, we find that networks trained on the same task remain closer to one another than to networks trained on different tasks. Thus, task-specific training appears to guide initially random networks toward distinct regions, or attractors, in structural network space. The earliest phase of training reveals an additional and unexpected phenomenon. Classification accuracy rises rapidly before the matched structural distances show strong task-specific separation, and before the global weight distribution visibly changes. Nevertheless, individual weight entries already begin to drift in a coordinated manner. This suggests that early learning may first operate through subtle, distributed adjustments that strongly affect function while leaving coarse network morphology almost unchanged. We treat this early morphogenesis as a first glimpse of a richer dynamical process that will be investigated in future work.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether neural networks with different random initializations converge to similar internal weight structures when trained on the same task, analogous to convergent evolution in biology. The authors introduce a matching-based framework for comparing MLPs in structural weight space, using permutation-invariant features and iterative Hungarian matching. They find that networks trained on the same task cluster together in structural space, and identify an early training phase where accuracy rises rapidly before structural separation emerges, suggesting learning begins through subtle distributed adjustments.
AI.motivation: The authors ask whether the biological phenomenon of convergent evolution has an analog in neural network training—do independently initialized networks trained on the same task converge to similar internal structures? This is technically challenging because hidden neurons can be permuted arbitrarily without changing function, making naive matrix comparisons misleading, so a principled matching framework is needed.
AI.method: The authors develop a matching-based framework for comparing multilayer perceptrons in structural weight space. Hidden neurons are first coarsely aligned using permutation-invariant features, then refined via iterative Hungarian matching. After alignment, structural distance metrics are used to compare networks, emphasizing task-relevant weight patterns. They apply this to ensembles of small MLPs trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST.
AI.result: Networks trained on the same task remain closer to one another than to networks trained on different tasks, indicating task-specific training guides networks toward distinct attractors in structural space. Additionally, during the earliest phase of training, classification accuracy rises rapidly before structural distances show task-specific separation, and individual weight entries begin to drift in a coordinated manner while coarse morphology stays nearly unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Task-specific training guides initially random networks toward distinct regions (attractors) in structural network space, demonstrating a form of convergent evolution in neural networks. The early phase of training operates through subtle, distributed weight adjustments that strongly affect function while leaving coarse network morphology mostly unchanged, offering a glimpse into a richer dynamical process for future investigation.

title: Convergent Evolution in Neural Representation Space: Emergent Order in Deep Belief Networks
summary: Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) learn hierarchical generative models without class supervision. Here, we ask whether this purely unsupervised process nevertheless organizes internal representations according to the unknown data classes. We analyze successive layers of DBNs trained on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST using the Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV), supervised probes applied only after training, a reconstruction-based measure of abstraction distance, effective dimensionality, and free sample generation. Remarkably, class-specific clustering generally increases with depth across datasets and network widths, although no label information is available during DBN training. Control experiments show that this effect depends on the learned feature structure and cannot be explained by random transformations, weight marginals, dimensionality reduction, or sigmoid saturation. The first hidden layers also frequently make class identity more accessible to linear and nonlinear probes. With greater depth, representations become increasingly compact and prototype-like as neurons acquire correlated feature directions. At the same time, GDV and probe accuracy reveal complementary aspects of class structure: improved average clustering can coexist with reduced accessibility for a few difficult class pairs. These findings demonstrate that layer-wise generative learning can spontaneously uncover and progressively amplify class-related structure in unlabeled data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether Deep Belief Networks (DBNs), trained purely unsupervised, spontaneously organize internal representations according to unknown data classes. Analyzing DBNs on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and KMNIST, the authors find that class-specific clustering generally increases with depth, with representations becoming more compact and prototype-like, even though no label information is used during training.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether purely unsupervised generative learning in DBNs can nevertheless organize internal representations according to unknown data classes, exploring whether class structure emerges spontaneously without any label supervision.
AI.method: The authors analyze successive layers of DBNs using multiple measures: the Generalized Discrimination Value (GDV), supervised probes applied only after training, a reconstruction-based measure of abstraction distance, effective dimensionality, and free sample generation. Control experiments rule out random transformations, weight marginals, dimensionality reduction, and sigmoid saturation as explanations.
AI.result: Class-specific clustering generally increases with depth across datasets and network widths. First hidden layers make class identity more accessible to linear and nonlinear probes. Deeper representations become increasingly compact and prototype-like with correlated feature directions. GDV and probe accuracy reveal complementary aspects: improved clustering can coexist with reduced accessibility for difficult class pairs.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise generative learning can spontaneously uncover and progressively amplify class-related structure in unlabeled data, demonstrating that unsupervised DBN training implicitly discovers class organization without any label supervision.

title: Simple evolution drives direct reciprocity to maximum payoff in social dilemmas
summary: Direct reciprocity is a mechanism for evolution of cooperation based on repeated interactions between the same individuals. Direct reciprocity can help natural selection to favor cooperators over defectors, but whether or not cooperation prevails depends on the details of the evolutionary dynamics. We describe simple processes of evolution that have the astonishing ability of driving direct reciprocity to maximum payoff in all social dilemmas which we study. The basic process is based on mutation and pairwise comparison. Mutation samples strategies near the boundary of the strategy space. Pairwise comparison includes a parameter for intensity of selection. For large population sizes, intermediate to high mutation rates and intermediate to strong intensities of selection, we find that the process leads to communities of strategies that reach maximum payoff in Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt and Harmony games. Maximum payoff in all four games is consistently achieved if players have access to memory-2 strategies. Memory-1 strategies have the capacity to resolve all four social dilemmas, but they are usually defeated by a ``Hold-trap'' in Snowdrift games.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a simple evolutionary process based on mutation and pairwise comparison can drive direct reciprocity to maximum payoff across all four major social dilemmas (Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, Harmony), achieving consistently optimal outcomes when players use memory-2 strategies, though memory-1 strategies still resolve all dilemmas but are typically defeated by a "Hold-trap" in Snowdrift games.
AI.motivation: Direct reciprocity enables cooperation evolution through repeated interactions, but whether cooperation prevails depends on the details of the underlying evolutionary dynamics. The authors seek to identify simple evolutionary processes that can reliably drive reciprocity to maximum payoff across diverse social dilemmas.
AI.method: The proposed process combines mutation and pairwise comparison dynamics. Mutation samples strategies near the boundary of the strategy space, while pairwise comparison includes a parameter controlling intensity of selection. The framework is applied to analyze behavior in Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, and Harmony games for both memory-1 and memory-2 strategies.
AI.result: For large population sizes, intermediate-to-high mutation rates, and intermediate-to-strong intensities of selection, the process drives strategy communities to maximum payoff in all four social dilemmas studied. Maximum payoff is consistently achieved with memory-2 strategies. Memory-1 strategies can resolve all four dilemmas but are usually defeated by a "Hold-trap" in Snowdrift games.
AI.conclusion: Evolutionary dynamics with mutation and pairwise comparison exhibit an astonishing capability to push direct reciprocity toward maximum payoff across all major social dilemma types, with memory-2 strategies proving consistently sufficient for optimal outcomes.

title: Errorless Irrationality: A unified computational account of the inverse base-rate effect across predictive, observational, and unsupervised procedures
summary: The inverse base-rate effect is a robust bias in how people resolve ambiguity between competing categories, and the most prominent theories explain it through prediction error. Across two experiments we progressively removed the elements of the predictive-learning design that supply such error signals: first by moving to observational learning, then to an unsupervised procedure in which category labels were not presented. The effect persisted--the irrational bias is independent of supervised learning procedures. We propose a new theory, OSCAR, that integrates core computational principles of the best-validated models and operates on self-generated feedback akin to pattern completion. OSCAR extends the learning dynamics underlying the response bias to observational and unsupervised procedures. Evaluated on a large preexisting supervised dataset in addition to the two new experiments reported here, OSCAR performs competitively against alternatives, and is the first model that reproduces the pattern of individual differences seen in humans across all three procedures. The model provides an explanation of hitherto unexplained eye-tracking data, something none of the alternative accounts provide.

AI.tldr: The inverse base-rate effect persists even when supervised learning signals are removed (observational and unsupervised learning), leading to a new model (OSCAR) that explains this bias through self-generated feedback akin to pattern completion.
AI.motivation: Existing theories explain the inverse base-rate effect through prediction error from supervised learning, but the paper investigates whether this bias persists when such error signals are progressively removed, testing the necessity of supervised learning procedures.
AI.method: Two experiments progressively remove supervised learning elements (observational learning, then unsupervised with no category labels). A new computational model, OSCAR, integrates principles from best-validated models and operates on self-generated feedback similar to pattern completion, evaluated on a large preexisting supervised dataset plus the two new experiments.
AI.result: The inverse base-rate effect persisted even without supervised learning signals, showing the bias is independent of supervised procedures. OSCAR performed competitively against alternative models, is the first to reproduce human individual differences across all three procedures, and uniquely explains previously unexplained eye-tracking data.
AI.conclusion: The inverse base-rate effect is more fundamental than supervised-learning-based theories suggest, and OSCAR provides a unified account spanning supervised, observational, and unsupervised learning while also explaining eye-tracking data that alternatives cannot.

title: PyOMES: an open-source framework for biochemical process modelling
summary: PyOMES is a Python-based, Open-source Modelling Environment for (bio)chemical process Simulation that aims to simplify the modelling of dynamic (including steady state) processes. This is done in a generalied, modular way to facilitate modelling a broad range of biological, chemical, and biochemical systems under a single modelling framework. PyOMES has been built to be accessible to a broad range of users - ranging from those with little modelling experience, such as experimentalists and students, through to more experienced power-users. Here, an introduction is provided to the PyOMES software including a summary of the design, architecture and vision. Use cases are then provided to demonstrate applicability of PyOMES to a number of (bio)chemical process modelling scenarios. Comparisons of predictions against existing benchmark software (i.e. PHREEQC) demonstrate the robustness of the package. Finally, a summary is provided of future directions for the PyOMES package - highlighting its establishment as a unified modelling framework and its potential for community-driven improvement as future developments.

AI.tldr: PyOMES is a Python-based, open-source modelling environment for simulating dynamic/steady-state biochemical and chemical processes. It provides a generalized, modular framework accessible to users from beginners to experts, validated against benchmark software like PHREEQC, and designed for community-driven development.
AI.motivation: To simplify the modelling of dynamic (including steady state) biochemical and chemical processes by providing a generalized, modular, and accessible framework under a single modelling environment, catering to users with varying levels of modelling experience.
AI.method: PyOMES adopts a generalized, modular design architecture built in Python, enabling flexible modelling of a broad range of biological, chemical, and biochemical systems. Validation is performed by comparing predictions against existing benchmark software (e.g., PHREEQC), and use cases demonstrate applicability across various (bio)chemical process modelling scenarios.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates PyOMES's applicability through multiple use cases in (bio)chemical process modelling, with predictions validated against benchmark software (PHREEQC) confirming the robustness of the package.
AI.conclusion: PyOMES is established as a unified modelling framework with strong potential for community-driven improvement and future development as an accessible, robust solution for biochemical and chemical process simulation.

title: MS-MLB: An Open Machine Learning Benchmark for Blood-Based MS Classification
summary: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is diagnosed through clinical assessment, magnetic resonance imaging, laboratory evidence when appropriate, and exclusion of better explanations. Blood RNA expression data may contain disease associated immune signal, but a blood RNA classifier cannot be treated as a replacement for clinical diagnosis. This paper presents MS-MLB (Multiple Sclerosis Machine Learning Benchmark), a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning based MS research classification from whole blood RNA expression data. MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort, converts it into an MS versus healthy control task, and evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage controlled pipeline that a researcher can rerun without reconfiguring the evaluation. The evaluation includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score. In the final benchmark summary, Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, with an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, $F_{1}$ score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050. Prior studies have applied machine learning to MS blood transcriptomic data, including PBMC stage classification and whole blood diagnostic signature modeling. The contribution here is different and narrower. To our knowledge, MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway built into the framework. The score is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated. The benchmark is accessible here: https://github.com/duckyquang/MS-MLB.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MS-MLB, a reproducible open benchmark for machine learning classification of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) versus healthy controls from whole blood RNA expression data (GSE17048 cohort). It evaluates multiple algorithms under a leakage-controlled pipeline with nested cross-validation, holdout sets, bootstrap confidence intervals, and calibration metrics, with Gradient Boosting achieving the best MS Research Score (93.83) on the holdout set.
AI.motivation: Multiple sclerosis diagnosis relies on clinical assessment and multiple modalities, but blood RNA expression data may carry disease-associated immune signals. The authors aim to provide a standardized, reproducible benchmark for ML-based MS research classification from whole blood RNA data, addressing the lack of a fair comparison framework in prior studies.
AI.method: MS-MLB uses the public GSE17048 cohort and converts it into an MS versus healthy control classification task. It evaluates multiple algorithms under a shared, leakage-controlled pipeline that includes nested cross-validation, an untouched stratified holdout set, bootstrap confidence intervals, ROC and precision-recall analysis, calibration measurement, and an exploratory MS Research Score.
AI.result: Gradient Boosting ranked first by MS Research Score on the holdout set, achieving an MS Research Score of 93.83, AUC-ROC of 0.989, sensitivity of 0.950, specificity of 0.778, F1 score of 0.927, and Brier score of 0.050.
AI.conclusion: MS-MLB is the first open benchmark focused on MS versus healthy control classification from GSE17048 whole blood RNA expression data with a documented external model submission pathway. The benchmark is intended for research comparison only and has not been clinically validated.

title: Toward a Dynamical Taxonomy of Insomnia: A Multiaxial Framework for Sleep-State Transitions and Architectural Failure
summary: Insomnia disorder is defined at the syndrome level, yet similar complaints can arise from different abnormalities in sleep regulation, state transition, state stabilization, spatial recruitment, architectural sequencing, and state perception. We propose a multiaxial dynamical framework whose principal contribution is organizational: a candidate profile is specified by the dynamical operation that fails, the sleep stage or boundary at which it fails, and its causal status. Objective sleep duration, age, circadian phase, comorbidity, medication exposure, and night-to-night variability are modifier/covariate dimensions rather than additional mechanistic classes. A local Landau-Ginzburg formalism, adopted from prior cortical and sleep-dynamics work, supplies a phenomenological language for nested hypotheses. Its relaxational form applies only to boundary-local dynamics under an approximate gradient description; non-gradient escape requires an action or quasipotential treatment, and whole-night REM-NREM sequencing requires reactive or oscillatory dynamics. Routine polysomnography usually identifies effective combinations rather than curvature, escape action, bias, noise, and relaxation separately. The strongest boundary-level evidence concerns sleep onset, where published results are consistent with bifurcation-like or bistable dynamics but do not yet exclude a driven smooth transition produced by the homeostatic-circadian ramp. The remaining operation classes are hypothesis-generating extensions. The taxonomy is judged by pragmatic utility, including improved communication, stratification, and prediction; the scalar-field implementation and specific dynamical profiles are separately falsifiable. The framework is a phenomenological organizing model rather than a new diagnosis, validated biomarker, or treatment-selection system.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multiaxial dynamical framework for classifying insomnia disorder by specifying which dynamical operation fails (e.g., sleep regulation, state transition, stabilization, spatial recruitment, sequencing, perception), at which sleep stage or boundary, and with what causal status. It adopts a Landau-Ginzburg formalism from physics to provide a phenomenological language for nested hypotheses, while treating factors like age, circadian phase, comorbidity, and medication as modifiers rather than separate mechanistic classes. The framework is presented as an organizational/phenomenological model for improved communication and stratification, not a validated diagnostic system.
AI.motivation: Insomnia is defined at the syndrome level, yet the same complaints can stem from fundamentally different underlying abnormalities in sleep regulation and dynamics. A unified organizational framework is needed to classify insomnia subtypes mechanistically, improving communication, stratification, and prediction beyond the current syndromic definitions.
AI.method: The authors propose a multiaxial dynamical framework where insomnia profiles are specified by three axes: (1) the dynamical operation that fails, (2) the sleep stage or boundary at which it fails, and (3) its causal status. They adopt a local Landau-Ginzburg formalism from prior cortical and sleep-dynamics work as a phenomenological language, distinguishing relaxational dynamics (for boundary-local phenomena), non-gradient escape (requiring action/quasipotential treatment), and reactive/oscillatory dynamics (for whole-night REM-NREM sequencing). Modifier dimensions include sleep duration, age, circadian phase, comorbidity, medication, and night-to-night variability.
AI.result: The strongest boundary-level evidence supports bifurcation-like or bistable dynamics at sleep onset, though a driven smooth transition from the homeostatic-circadian ramp cannot yet be excluded. The remaining dynamical operation classes remain hypothesis-generating. Routine polysomnography can typically identify effective combinations of parameters but cannot separate curvature, escape action, bias, noise, and relaxation individually. The taxonomy is judged by pragmatic utility and the scalar-field implementation and specific profiles are separately falsifiable.
AI.conclusion: The multiaxial dynamical framework serves as a phenomenological organizing model for insomnia rather than a new diagnosis, biomarker, or treatment-selection system. Its principal contribution is organizational—providing a structured way to specify candidate insomnia mechanisms that can improve communication and stratification while remaining open to empirical validation and falsification at both the implementation and profile levels.

title: A Quantum Circuit Framework for Protein Ensemble-Level Energetics
comment: Please see github repo https://github.com/pra-ashok/QProtSim for code and supplementary information. A Pypi package qprotsim is also available at https://pypi.org/project/qprotsim/
summary: Proteins occupy heterogeneous free-energy landscapes in which high-entropy ensembles converge toward compact, low-energy basins with multiple sub-states. Molecular dynamics can access these landscapes at atomic resolution, but exhaustive sampling remains computationally demanding. Meanwhile, most quantum approaches target only single optimal structures, leaving full ensemble energetic heterogeneity unexplored. We introduce a residue-level, gate-based quantum circuit framework for coarse-graining protein thermodynamics. Each amino acid is represented as a two-state qubit (stabilised vs. excited solvation state) based on residue solvation energetics. A structure-informed entanglement block then encodes covalent and non-covalent contacts using parameterised controlled gates, embedding correlations across the residue-interaction network. Sampling the circuit ($\sim 10^6$ measurements) yields binary thermodynamic microstates used to compute protein energy distributions, residue-level statistical couplings, energetic sensitivities, and information gains relative to total free energy. We showcase the framework on the benchmark Trp-cage miniprotein 1L2Y (TC5b) and 9GDL, a disulfide-stabilised Trp-cage-fortified exenatide chimera. For 1L2Y, the circuit reproduces a structured, folding-funnel-like energy distribution. Comparative analysis with 9GDL reveals shifts in global energy distributions and residue-level stability profiles. Coupling and information-theoretic analyses localise residues associated with ensemble reorganisation, while multi-body couplings show the circuit resolves both direct and indirect statistical correlations. This framework expands quantum protein modelling beyond single-structure optimisation toward ensemble-level characterisation, capturing key features of rugged energy landscapes to guide protein design, mutation mapping, and allosteric pathway identification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a residue-level, gate-based quantum circuit framework for coarse-graining protein thermodynamics, representing each amino acid as a two-state qubit and using parameterized controlled gates to encode structural contacts. The framework samples the circuit to compute energy distributions and statistical couplings, demonstrated on Trp-cage proteins 1L2Y and 9GDL, capturing folding-funnel-like energy landscapes and localizing residues associated with ensemble reorganisation—enabling ensemble-level quantum protein modeling beyond single-structure optimization.
AI.motivation: Proteins exist in heterogeneous free-energy landscapes with multiple sub-states, but molecular dynamics sampling is computationally demanding and most quantum approaches only target single optimal structures, leaving ensemble energetic heterogeneity unexplored.
AI.method: Each amino acid is represented as a two-state qubit (stabilised vs. excited solvation state) based on residue solvation energetics. A structure-informed entanglement block uses parameterised controlled gates to encode covalent and non-covalent contacts. Circuit sampling (~10^6 measurements) yields binary thermodynamic microstates for computing energy distributions, statistical couplings, sensitivities, and information gains.
AI.result: On benchmark 1L2Y (TC5b) and 9GDL (a disulfide-stabilised Trp-cage-fortified exenatide chimera), the circuit reproduces a structured folding-funnel-like energy distribution for 1L2Y. Comparative analysis with 9GDL reveals shifts in global energy distributions and residue-level stability profiles. Coupling and information-theoretic analyses localise residues associated with ensemble reorganisation, and multi-body couplings resolve both direct and indirect statistical correlations.
AI.conclusion: The framework expands quantum protein modelling beyond single-structure optimisation toward ensemble-level characterisation, capturing key features of rugged energy landscapes to guide protein design, mutation mapping, and allosteric pathway identification.

title: Two base rates, two weights: base-rate neglect has a second axis
comment: 33 pages, 14 figures. Code to reproduce all formal claims and figures: https://osf.io/9qvbr/
summary: Base-rate neglect is usually treated as one mistake: giving the prior too little weight. Turning the co-occurrences you see into a useful judgment, though, means correcting for two base rates, not one. The first is the familiar prior, how common the outcome is. The second is how common the cue itself is. Those are two separate mistakes, and a learner can make either one alone. Under-correcting the prior is classical base-rate neglect; under-correcting the cue is the cue-density effect of contingency learning, long studied but not previously recognised as a kind of base-rate neglect. We write both corrections as two weights in one Bayesian equation. The task decides which weight it can measure: the cue-frequency weight appears only in graded ratings, because a two-choice test cancels it. At their extremes the two weights recover familiar quantities: base-rate neglect, the signal-detection criterion, the contiguity/sensitivity/validity triple, and the "lift" measure of causal strength. The same cue-frequency weight also sits inside six standard learning-and-memory models; they seem to agree, but only because the usual experiments squeeze the data into a form where they cannot disagree. Above all, the two neglects should be separately manipulable: an experimenter can move one without moving the other. That is a double dissociation, and a one-parameter account cannot produce it. That prediction is the framework's centre, and it has not yet been tested. This paper lays out the framework and the rating experiment that would settle it; a companion paper fits the two weights to an existing colour-flavour dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper argues that base-rate neglect is not a single error but two distinct mistakes: under-correcting for the prior (outcome frequency) and under-correcting for cue frequency (the cue-density effect). Both can be represented as two weights in one Bayesian equation, appear only in graded ratings (not two-choice tests), and should be separately manipulable—a double dissociation prediction that a one-parameter account cannot produce and has not yet been tested.
AI.motivation: Base-rate neglect is traditionally treated as a single mistake—giving the prior too little weight. The authors argue this is incomplete: making useful judgments from co-occurrences requires correcting for two base rates—outcome frequency (the familiar prior) and cue frequency—which are two separate mistakes that can occur independently. The cue-density effect has long been studied but never recognized as a form of base-rate neglect, and existing models may agree only because experimental designs prevent them from disagreeing.
AI.method: The authors formulate both corrections as two weights in a single Bayesian equation. They show that the task choice determines which weight can be measured: the cue-frequency weight appears only in graded ratings because two-choice tests cancel it. They demonstrate that the framework's extremes recover familiar quantities (base-rate neglect, signal-detection criterion, contiguity/sensitivity/validity triple, and the "lift" measure of causal strength), and that the same cue-frequency weight sits inside six standard learning-and-memory models. They propose a rating experiment to test the central prediction of double dissociation.
AI.result: The framework unifies classical base-rate neglect with the cue-density effect as two separable weights in one Bayesian equation. It shows that existing models appear to agree only because standard experiments constrain data in ways that prevent disagreement. The central prediction—that the two neglects should be separately manipulable (a double dissociation)—has not yet been tested; the paper lays out the rating experiment that would settle it, with a companion paper fitting the two weights to a colour-flavour dataset.
AI.conclusion: Base-rate neglect should be reconceptualized as two distinct errors—prior under-correction and cue under-correction—rather than a single mistake. This framework generates a falsifiable double-dissociation prediction that distinguishes it from one-parameter accounts, and the proposed rating experiment (along with companion empirical fitting) will determine whether the framework holds.

title: Multiparametric MRI Radiomics and Machine Learning Framework for Predicting Treatment Response in Glioblastoma
summary: Distinguishing True Progression (TP) from Pseudo-Progression (PsP) after chemoradiotherapy remains a major diagnostic challenge in GBM, as both entities present near-identical appearances on conventional contrast-enhanced post-treatment MRI. This distinction carries substantial clinical weight, since TP and PsP demand divergent management yet cannot be reliably separated on routine imaging alone. We investigated whether radiomic features derived from a parsimonious, voxel-wise pharmacokinetic model of dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI, combined with MGMT status, could discriminate between the two. The cohort comprised 82 adults with IDH-wildtype GBM who developed a new contrast-enhancing lesion within six months of chemoradiotherapy; classification (53 TP, 29 PsP) was established by histopathology where available (n=52) and modified RANO criteria otherwise (n=30). At every voxel, contrast-concentration time courses were fitted to five candidate pharmacokinetic models, and the best fit was retained by AIC minimisation, yielding parsimonious Ktrans, Ve, Vp, and taui maps adapting to local heterogeneity rather than a single fixed model across the tumour. Following segmentation, 1,073 radiomic descriptors were extracted and reduced via Mann-Whitney U filtering and Elastic Net, then used to train five classifiers across four feature configurations. A Random Forest classifier combining parsimonious DCE-MRI radiomics with MGMT status achieved the best discrimination (mean AUC 0.89, sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.76, F1 0.90), outperforming features without MGMT (0.84), a T1-post-contrast baseline (0.72), and a single-model extended-Tofts analysis (0.68). Shape and textural descriptors of the Ktrans map, with tumour volume, were the strongest predictors, MGMT contributing a smaller, independent effect. Allowing the model to vary voxel-wise improves non-invasive discrimination.

AI.tldr: This study uses parsimonious voxel-wise pharmacokinetic modeling of DCE-MRI radiomics combined with MGMT status to discriminate true progression (TP) from pseudo-progression (PsP) in IDH-wildtype GBM patients. A Random Forest classifier achieved mean AUC 0.89, outperforming baselines and demonstrating improved non-invasive discrimination.
AI.motivation: Distinguishing true progression from pseudo-progression after chemoradiotherapy in GBM is clinically critical yet challenging, as both appear nearly identical on conventional post-treatment MRI. Reliable non-invasive discrimination is needed since these two entities require divergent clinical management.
AI.method: 82 adults with IDH-wildtype GBM and new contrast-enhancing lesions within 6 months post-chemoradiotherapy were studied (53 TP, 29 PsP). Voxel-wise contrast-concentration time courses were fitted to five candidate pharmacokinetic models with best fit retained via AIC minimization, yielding parsimonious Ktrans, Ve, Vp, and taui maps. 1,073 radiomic descriptors were extracted and reduced via Mann-Whitney U filtering and Elastic Net, then used to train five classifiers across four feature configurations.
AI.result: A Random Forest classifier combining parsimonious DCE-MRI radiomics with MGMT status achieved the best performance (mean AUC 0.89, sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.76, F1 0.90), outperforming radiomics without MGMT (0.84), T1-post-contrast baseline (0.72), and single-model extended-Tofts analysis (0.68). Ktrans map shape and textural descriptors with tumor volume were strongest predictors.
AI.conclusion: Voxel-wise adaptive model selection for DCE-MRI radiomics significantly improves non-invasive discrimination between TP and PsP in GBM, with MGMT status providing a small independent additive effect.

title: THBKG: A Temporal Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Decision-Aligned Clinical Advancement Prediction
summary: Inadequate target--disease linkage accounts for 40--50\% of Phase~II efficacy failures, so anticipating which programmes will advance would let sponsors back the hypotheses most likely to reach patients. What a programme can be judged on is the evidence that supported its linkage \emph{when it entered the clinic}. No existing biomedical knowledge graph allows that evidence profile to be assembled as of a past date. We present the Temporal Heterogeneous Biomedical Knowledge Graph (THBKG), which describes and predicts therapeutic target--disease links through time: 110,396 entities and 11.1M edges across nineteen relation types, each edge carrying the year its evidence changed, so a pair's profile can be recovered as it stood when its own decision fell due. On this graph we define a decision-aligned benchmark that predicts, for a target--disease pair entering Phase~II, whether it advances to Phase~III on evidence datable before that decision. Graph propagation over the THBKG outranks every direct-evidence reference scored under the same decision-aligned protocol, reaching a relative success of 4.3--4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area. The gain concentrates on the 72.8\% of pairs with no direct target--disease evidence at their decision point, where a direct-edge model has nothing to read: the encoders still rank five- to sixfold above chance, recovering the signal by propagating over the intervening biology. Adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph decomposes each prediction into the evidence landscape behind the hypothesis for explainable prediction. We release the THBKG as a continually updated substrate for studying therapeutic target hypotheses by retrospective validation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces THBKG, a temporal heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph with 110,396 entities and 11.1M time-stamped edges, designed to reconstruct target-disease evidence profiles as they existed at past decision points. A decision-aligned benchmark shows graph propagation outperforms direct-evidence methods (relative success 4.3-4.5 at top ten pairs), particularly for the 72.8% of pairs lacking direct evidence, by propagating signal through intermediary biology while enabling explainable predictions.
AI.motivation: 40-50% of Phase II efficacy failures stem from inadequate target-disease linkage. To help sponsors back the most promising hypotheses, the authors need to evaluate programmes based on evidence available at the time of clinical entry, but no existing biomedical knowledge graph supports reconstructing evidence profiles as of a past date.
AI.method: The authors build THBKG, a temporal heterogeneous biomedical knowledge graph with 110,396 entities, 11.1M edges across 19 relation types, where each edge records the year its evidence changed. They define a decision-aligned benchmark predicting Phase II-to-III advancement based on evidence datable before the decision, and apply graph propagation over the knowledge graph, adapting a path-based explainer to the decision-time subgraph.
AI.result: Graph propagation over THBKG achieves a relative success of 4.3-4.5 at the top ten pairs per therapeutic area, outperforming all direct-evidence reference models. The gain concentrates on the 72.8% of pairs lacking direct target-disease evidence, where the encoders rank 5-6x above chance by exploiting intervening biology.
AI.conclusion: Temporal knowledge graphs effectively capture the evolving evidence landscape for therapeutic target hypotheses, enabling retrospective validation and explainable prediction even when direct evidence is absent, and the THBKG is released as a continually updated substrate for such studies.

title: EpiBench: Can LLMs Understand Epitopes for Antibody Drug Discovery?
summary: Epitopes determine where antibodies bind antigens and shape downstream therapeutic properties such as functional blockade and escape resistance, making epitope understanding central to antibody drug discovery. Although large language models (LLMs) have shown strong biomedical reasoning ability, it remains unclear whether they can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing epitope resources typically focus on isolated prediction tasks or rely on specialized structural settings, while general protein benchmarks do not evaluate epitope-centered decisions across the antibody development workflow. To address this gap, we introduce EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, and automatically scorable benchmark for evaluating epitope reasoning in LLMs. EpiBench contains 1,609 curated samples grounded in structural antibody--antigen contacts, curated functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements. It covers five connected tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment, with controlled sampling to reduce shortcut-based evaluation artifacts. We evaluate nine general-purpose LLMs and analyze their behavior through task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection. The results show that current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning. Therefore, EpiBench provides a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs toward reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EpiBench, a closed-book, sequence-based, and automatically scorable benchmark for evaluating epitope reasoning capabilities of large language models in antibody discovery. It contains 1,609 curated samples across five connected tasks and evaluates nine general-purpose LLMs, finding they capture partial epitope signals but lack antibody-specific sequence grounding and biologically grounded reasoning.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs show strong biomedical reasoning, it is unclear whether they can infer epitope information directly from antigen and antibody sequences. Existing epitope resources focus on isolated prediction tasks or specialized structural settings, while general protein benchmarks do not evaluate epitope-centered decisions across the antibody development workflow.
AI.method: The authors build EpiBench with 1,609 curated samples grounded in structural antibody-antigen contacts, curated functional B-cell assays, and deep mutational scanning escape measurements. The benchmark covers five connected tasks: targetable region discovery, antibody-conditioned epitope identification, epitope binning, functional epitope assessment, and antibody escape assessment, with controlled sampling to reduce shortcut-based evaluation artifacts. Nine general-purpose LLMs are evaluated with task-specific baselines, antigen length stratification, explicit-reasoning comparison, and failure-mode inspection.
AI.result: Current LLMs capture partial epitope-related signals but remain limited in antibody-specific sequence grounding, long-context residue localization, and biologically grounded reasoning.
AI.conclusion: EpiBench provides a diagnostic testbed for measuring and improving sequence-aware biomedical LLMs toward reliable LLM-assisted antibody discovery.
